It all depends on how you view things, what depicts being successful, what depicts a person doing better than another, and so on.

For example, the core issue in how society treats men vs how it treats women is that society views men as workers, as fighters, thinkers, and so on, while society views women as the caretakers, the teachers, and so on.

Women and Children are considered the "body" or the "future" of society,to be protected and grown, while men are the weapons, arms, tools, etc, that are used to do exactly that.

Such a structure grew in a time when society didn't have simple living. Women would regularly die of childbirth, all work was the sort of work you see being done in coal mines today. And men are hands down better at doing that sort of work. Evolution doesn't need the man to live beyond his first kid, so the man could go and do the "tough" or risky jobs without risk to the group. You see it in the structure of the male vs the female body, and it is possible similar specializations exist in the mind, although that is debated.

However, modern day society no longer relies so much on that hard work. That doesn't exactly make men useless, but it does make men no longer nearly as specialized for working. Because of this, and because of modern medicine and so on, women are far more capable of supporting themselves and doing the "hard" work that builds society and produces things. It's no longer risky or dangerous to work an office job. Being three hundred pounds of muscle aren't going to help you write a paper.

Before I start, I want to point out my understanding on the topic is limited to a couple of classes I took about a year ago. For those of you who want me to get straight to the point and answer the question, here it is: I believe that depending on the definition of "patriarchy" there it may exist in modern western society, but I don't think that's relevant; at the end of the day it's impossible to isolate any one specific event and attribute "the patriarchy" as its cause, and in many ways the idea of a patriarchy isn't useful because it's inherently not falsifiable under most definitions.

From what I recall, the patriarchy is the idea that because we live in a world which has its roots in a very sexist (among other forms of discrimination) time, our cultural values and more broadly the way our world was shaped are inherently sexist because of their roots in the enlightenment. For example, though legally men and women must be treated equally in the workforce by their employers, men and women have different pressures put upon them by their friends and family. The pressure to, say, start a family and be a stay-at-home mom for example, acts as a force to push women out of the workplace. On the flip side the pressure to have a successful career pushes men to stay in the workforce. Both of these cultural pressures are said to have their roots in the patriarchy. Another argument is that the physical world we live in and the way it's designed harks back to a time where city planners, architects, etc. were all well-educated, rich white men and therefore the very space we live in puts different pressure and expectations unfairly on people who aren't rich and white and men.

Of course, I think that's bullshit. To attribute our culture only to the patriarchy of the enlightenment is a ridiculous oversimplification; it must be. It doesn't take into account the effects of other cultures that have become bigger and bigger parts of our lives recently. It doesn't take into account huge historic events that changed the way we think or feel.

So, let's bring all this back to my original criticism of those who blame the patriarchy for... well, for really anything at all. Yes, the very real sexism that women suffered in the past is a part of our history and a part of our culture. However it's impossible to look at any specific event or perceived act of discrimination and say "This was because of the patriarchy". It's not even possible to look at trends and attribute them definitively to the patriarchy because, of course, we don't have anything else to compare to.

That's why I categorically reject claims where the patriarchy is blamed. It's a scapegoat that anything can be pinned on without proof.

Just wanted to share a story I came across about so called "organic" farming practices. I live in a rural part of the US with tons of "organic", conventional, and grass-fed pasture-raised quality non certified farms for miles around. Recently on a trip to a farm where I buy my food I encountered an acquaintance who had recently contracted on some repairs for an "organic" Turkey farm with distribution regionally. What he described was pretty shocking.

The Turkeys are packed together in a huge building so tight they cannot really move, and the air around them is stale and smells like rotting carcass.They are so diseased that many of them simply collapse and die when they are being cleared out on the way to the slaughter. He said many of the carcasses ooze a green pus that looks like guacamole. The place also runs propane tanks and the poor turkeys get to breath that gas in everyday until they are moved out for slaughter. He said once they are cleared out the place pumps the facility with formaldehyde to sterilize everything for the next batch of Turkeys.

He also said when they found out he raised free-range chickens on his own property at home, he was no longer allowed to be within a hundred yards of the premises, because "free-range chickens transmit diseases that will affect their turkeys". He also mentioned, if they wanted to be certified as "free-range" it would be as simple as opening up the back doors of the building to an area immediately surrounded by fencing.

All this from a USDA certified organic Turkey farm.

Of course I can't personally corroborate this information, but take it as a warning to buy locally and know the farms you are buying from. Organic certification means practically nothing, especially when it comes to livestock.
